name: Okunjan and Kawarrangg, two of the four 'Kunjen dialects'
confidence_why: One first-hand description, checked against the source; 1 other work consulted does not discuss stress.
catalog_citation: Sommer, Bruce A. 1969. Kunjen phonology: synchronic and diachronic. Pacific Linguistics B-11. Canberra: Australian National University. DOI 10.15144/PL-B11 (ANU Open Research copy, hdl 1885/146443).
catalog_locator: Sec. 2.2 'Olgol, Okunjan, Kawarrangg', pp. 31-32; governing rule sec. 2.1 'Oykangand: Stress Pattern', pp. 29-30; domain sec. 2.0/2.1 p. 28; informants sec. 0.3 p. 6; dialect list p. 15.
catalog_quote: The remarks already made on the structure and stress pattern of Oykangand words also apply in general to the other dialects. Interesting exceptions that became evident in the corpora follow. ... OKUNJAN The vowel phenomenon observed in Olgol was also recorded in Okunjan, but only for mono-syllables which would otherwise end in a stop, l or r. The stress remains unchanged ... KAWARRANGG All words in phrase final position are terminated by a vowel, which like that in Okunjan varies considerably as to its voicing quality. [Oykangand rule, pp. 29-30] By contrast, there is evidence in Kunjen for a strong phonological pressure against this stress pattern. Stress is not predictable in the case of words of more than two syllables. ... Words of two syllables are invariably stressed on the final syllable ... Words of three syllables may be stressed on either the ultimate or penultimate syllable. A survey of dictionary entries revealed no statistically preferred pattern: the two word types were numerically almost identical. Although no two lexical items in the language are differentiated solely on the basis of stress, several sub-minimal pairs are evident among three syllable words ... Words of four and five syllables are most commonly the result of affixation or compounding. Stress may occur on any of the last three syllables of the word, but uninflected forms are frequently stressed on the final syllable.
world_status: statement found in an open source

new_statements.second_reader_evidence: File (76 pp. ANU Open Research copy of PL B-11) opened with extracted text. Every quoted piece is present verbatim at the stated locators (scanned spacing aside): printed p. 31 = p. 35, section '2.2. OLGOL, OKUNJAN, KAWARRANGG': 'The remarks already made on the structure and stress pattern of Oykangand words also apply in general to the other dialects. Interesting exceptions that became evident in the corpora follow.'; printed p. 32 = p. 36, OKUNJAN paragraph: 'The vowel phenomenon observed in Olgol was also recorded in Okunjan, but only for mono-syllables which would otherwise end in a stop, l or r. The stress remains unchanged' (examples [ara]~[arA] 'hand', [aytYaA]~[aytYA] 'food'), then…
new_statements.rule_in_words: One primary stress per phonological word (1-5 syllables), never on the initial syllable in polysyllables: disyllables are always stressed on the final syllable; trisyllables on the final or the penult, lexically (no statistical preference, sub-minimal pairs exist); four- and five-syllable words on any of the last three syllables, uninflected forms most often final. Sommer states this for Oykangand and extends it 'in general' to Okunjan (= Ogh Undjan) and Kawarrangg; the only dialect-specific stress remark is that Okunjan phrase-final echo vowels on monosyllables do not attract stress ('the stress remains unchanged'), unlike Olgol where the added vowel takes the stress.
new_statements.secondary_stress: None described. Reduplicated/compound grammatical words 'retain stress on both elements of the compound' and are treated as two phonological words (p. 30).
new_statements.exceptions: Okunjan: monosyllables that would end in a stop, l or r get an additional vowel in phrase-final position, stress unchanged; Kawarrangg: all phrase-final words end in a (variably voiced) vowel; Olgol (not this language): the added final vowel takes the stress, though some Olgol and a few Oykangand speakers keep stress on the initial syllable. Phrase-initial function words lose their initial vowel. Okunjan and Kawarrangg corpora are small (one Kawarrangg speaker; data elicited through Oykangand, p. 6, 73).
new_statements.domain_note: Word level: 'The phonological word.. consists of from one to five syllables; stress characterizes the nuclear syllable' (p. 28); phrase stress and intonation are treated separately in ch. 1. The echo-vowel remarks concern phrase-final (citation/isolation) position.
new_statements.identity_note: Sommer 1969 treats Okunjan (= Ogh Undjan / Ogunyjan) and Kawarrangg as two of the four 'Kunjen' dialects alongside Oykangand and Olgol (kunj1245, already in the catalog with the same source, classification lexical). The stress description is written for Oykangand (oyka1239 / kunj1245) and extended to Okunjan and Kawarrangg only 'in general', from small corpora (two Okunjan informants, one Kawarrangg speaker, elicited through Oykangand). Glottolog separates kawa1290 (dialects Kawarrang, Ogh Undjan) from Kunjen, so this is a same-source, cross-dialect attribution rather than a dedicated description; Sommer's 1997 Ogh Undjan sketch (Ethnografix, 58 pp.) is the dialect-specific work and was not locatable.

sources.note: p. 485: Ogunyjan listed among languages with historical stress shift from first to second syllable, but reports Alpher (1976:86-7) arguing that a stress-shift analysis of Ogunyjan and Oykangand-Olgol is not possible because V2 has been reduced or deleted (in Ogunyjan also in closed syllables); quotes Alpher 1976:87 on 'Uw-El' possibly shifting stress to V2 and back to V1. Diachronic and second-hand; no synchronic Ogh Undjan stress rule.
